# **Project Proposal**

## **Project Title**

Burned Area Detection in Northern Portugal from Sentinel-2 Imagery Using an EfficientNet-B2 U-Net Change-Detection Model

## **Project Category**

Image segmentation (bi-temporal change detection) applied to remote sensing; Burned-area mapping using Sentinel-2 Imagery.

## **Team Members**

* Hannah Nathanson: 129381  
* Danilo III Ortañez Gonzales: 29225

## **Project Plan**

### **Problem Statement**

Wildfires are one of the most damaging and recurrent hazards in Portugal, and timely, spatially accurate burned area maps underpin a cascade of critical downstream responses. Instituto da Conservação da Natureza e das Florestas (ICNF) currently produces authoritative burned-area perimeters (`ardida`) through manual satellite image interpretation, a process whose lag between fire occurrence and published polygon directly delays aerial firefighting resource allocation, emergency logistics, and legal and insurance triggers. A model that reliably reproduces this delineation from Sentinel-2 imagery alone would reduce that lag and provide a scalable alternative to manual mapping. Beyond immediate response, accurate burned perimeters are the entry point for post-fire erosion and flood risk modelling: burned soils lose their infiltration capacity and become highly erodible, so the spatial precision of the burn boundary propagates directly into debris-flow early warning systems and hydrological damage assessments. This project applies a pre-trained EfficientNet-B2 U-Net change-detection model, developed by the MLC research group for 10-band Sentinel-2 surface reflectance, to map burned areas across tile T29TPG in northeastern Portugal. Model predictions are assessed against ICNF's 2025 burned-area polygons, providing a spatially explicit accuracy assessment on Portuguese data.

### **Challenges**

This project faces four main challenges:

1. **Scalability to a full tile.** The predict function operates on single 256×256 chips, but the study area is a year-long HDF5 data cube; naive loading would exhaust memory and run times must stay practical.  
2. **Cloud cover and swath gaps.** Sentinel-2 time series are interrupted by clouds and orbit-edge gaps; per-scene quality filtering using the completeness categories computed in the data-exploration stage is a prerequisite to any chip-level inference.  
3. **Before/after pair selection.** The model compares a pre-fire chip against a post-fire chip, so prediction quality depends on choosing cloud-free acquisitions that bracket each fire event as closely as possible in time.  
4. **Validation design: ground-truth rasterisation and class imbalance.** Turning ICNF fire boundaries into per pixel labels on the HDF5 chip grid requires careful rasterisation to avoid label leakage at polygon boundaries.

### **Dataset**

The project draws on two datasets, both already in hand: Sentinel-2 imagery for 2025 over northeastern Portugal and ICNF’s official 2025 burned-area records. In this study, the Sentinel-2 imagery is the model’s input, while the ICNF records provide both the fire perimeters used as ground truth for validating the model and the event dates used to select pre- and post-fire scenes.

***Study Area***

The study area is located inside the bounds of Sentinel-2 tile T29TPG in Northeastern Portugal, as shown in Figure 1\. The tile spans the Portugal-Spain border, and in this study, the analysis will only cover areas within the Portuguese territory, which is roughly half of the tile’s full extent. This area corresponds to the Trás-os-Montes region, specifically districts of Bragança and Vila Real, a fire-prone landscape of shrubland, pine and oak forest stands and agricultural areas.

***Sentinel-2 Imagery***

This study will use Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from tile T29TPG in northeastern Portugal for the year 2025\. The imagery is stored in a single HDF5 file, where the main array has a shape of (79, 10, 62,849,024), corresponding to timestamps, bands (B2–B12), and pixels. The dataset contains 79 scenes acquired between 13 January and 29 December 2025, i.e., roughly one scene every five days. Each scene includes ten spectral bands (B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B8A, B11, B12), spanning the visible, red-edge, near-infrared, and short-wave infrared regions, all at 10 m spatial resolution. Only the portion of the tile within continental Portugal is included. The entire array is divided into chunks with a shape of (12, 10, 65,536). In simple terms, each chunk corresponds to one chip (256 × 256 pixels) with all ten bands for 12 consecutive scenes.

***Reference Data from ICNF***

Fire event ground truth comes from the official burned area records of the ICNF. The data set is a shapefile (ardida\_2025.shp) with 2,084 fire perimeters mapped for mainland Portugal in 2025, in the national reference system ETRS89 / Portugal TM06 (EPSG:3763). Each polygon includes the official fire code, start and end date and time, event duration, district, municipality, parish, cause class, and burned area in hectares, split into forest, shrubland, and farmland. The total mapped area (AreaHaSIG) is used as the event size. After clipping to tile T29TPG, 182 fire events fall inside the study area, 15 of which are larger than 65 ha. These large events, and their end dates, define the reference set to choose pre-fire and post-fire Sentinel-2 scenes.

### **Method or Algorithm**

***Deep Learning Model***

The model is a pre-trained U-Net with an EfficientNet-B2 encoder (\~10M parameters, estimated F1 ≈ 0.94 on held-out data), provided by the research group focusing on development of a deep learning model for vegetation change detection headed by Prof. Manuel Campagnolo via a standardised `predict(before_chip, after_chip, path_to_weights)` interface. Both input chips are 10x256x256 uint16 arrays containing surface reflectance values in the range 0–10000 across the ten Sentinel-2 bands B2–B12 ( with NoData encoded as 65535\. Each input is a 10×256×256 uint16 image chip of surface reflectance (values from 0 to 10,000; NoData \= 65,535). Two chips are stacked into one 20-channel input, so the encoder sees both dates at the same time and learns to compare them on its own.

All preprocessing is done inside the predict function. It first converts the uint16 values to 8-bit using a per-band percentile stretch, then normalises them. Because of this, the pipeline only needs to send the raw reflectance chips. The model output is a binary 256×256 mask, where 0 means background and 1 means burned. The model is used strictly for inference: no training or fine-tuning is performed in this project.

***Inference Pipeline*** 

The inference pipeline aims to apply the chip-level predict function into the tile-wide Sentinel-2 imagery to detect burned areas. The pipeline stages are as follows:

1. **Sentinel-2 imagery screening.** Usable acquisitions are identified from the per-scene cloud-cover and clear-pixel statistics stored in the cube, yielding a calendar of clear scenes. A maximum cloud-fraction threshold (to be tuned during development) defines which scenes are eligible for pairing; finer per-chip screening is deferred to stage 3\.  
2. **Pair Selection.** For each major ICNF fire event, the closest eligible acquisitions before its start date and after its end date are chosen, bracketing the fire as tightly as the cloud record allows.  
3. **Batched Inference.** Chip pairs are read from the HDF5 file, screened for missing data, and passed through the predict function in batches with the weights loaded once. Different ways of deploying the model will be tested, such as reading chunk-aligned data per chip and loading the whole scene at once, as well as using different inference batch sizes. These options will be compared by runtime and peak memory, and the setup with the best performance will be used for the production runs.  
4. **Mosaicking.** Chip predictions are reassembled on the tile grid and exported as a georeferenced burned-area map (GeoTIFF, EPSG:32629) for evaluation against the rasterised ICNF reference.

Each stage will be implemented as an independent, testable module, with the prediction model as a swappable component behind the agreed interface.

### **Evaluation**

Model predictions are evaluated against ICNF’s official ardida\_2025 records: fire perimeters are rasterised to the 10 m chip grid to produce per-pixel reference labels, with polygon interiors eroded by one pixel before rasterisation to exclude ambiguous mixed pixels at burn boundaries. Comparison is restricted to what the model could actually observe, because evaluation uses the image pair bracketing each fire, and chips marked unobserved by the pipeline (cloud or missing data) are excluded from scoring rather than counted as correct rejections.

Because burned pixels are a small fraction of the tile, overall accuracy is not used as a primary metric: a trivial classifier that predicts no burned pixels would score above 95% yet have zero utility (Campagnolo, T6). Evaluation instead centres on the confusion matrix and the metrics derived from its four cells (TP, TN, FP, FN), all computed on the burned class. The primary metrics are precision (complement of commission error), recall (complement of omission error), F1 score computed on the burned class only, and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). MCC is preferred as the single-number summary because it incorporates all four confusion matrix entries and is invariant to class swapping, making it the most balanced measure for an imbalanced binary problem (Campagnolo, T6; Raschka, Ch. 6). Since the model outputs a hard binary prediction rather than a probability, threshold-dependent analysis replaces ROC/AUC. Per-acquisition metrics will also be reported to assess how performance varies with scene cloud fraction and the temporal gap between the before/after acquisition and the actual fire date.
